findings.claim: a cool-down gradually lowers heart rate, removes metabolic waste products from working muscles and aids recovery
findings.truth: An active cool-down can help heart rate and breathing return towards resting levels. It may accelerate lactate clearance from blood, but it has not been shown to clear waste from muscle or improve most recovery outcomes.
findings.evidence: PubMed PMID 29663142, review of active cool-downs; spec 1.3.1 requires the structure and function of warm-up and cool-down.

findings.claim: more than roughly 10% per week as a general guideline
findings.truth: There is no reliable universal 10% weekly threshold for safe training-load progression. Progression should be gradual and tailored to the performer and activity.
findings.evidence: PubMed PMID 30534459 found very limited evidence and no difference in injury risk between 10% and 24% weekly volume increases.

findings.claim: Each principle addresses a different risk: specificity guards against wasted effort, overload drives adaptation, reversibility reminds us that fitness is temporary, variance keeps athletes engaged, and individual needs ensure the programme fits the person, not just the sport.
findings.truth: The specification requires specificity, overload through intensity, frequency and duration, progression, and variance. It does not list reversibility or individual needs as principles. Option A: rebuild the lesson, questions and glossary around the four required principles. Option B: retain the extra ideas only as clearly labelled enrichment and add progression.

findings.claim: There are two main types specified.
findings.truth: The specification requires flexibility training but does not prescribe static stretching and PNF as two named types or as an exam requirement. They can be presented as enrichment without calling them specified.
PNF includes both assisted and self-performed hold-relax and contract-relax techniques, so a partner is not always required.
findings.evidence: PubMed PMID 29474101, systematic review comparing assisted and self hold-relax and contract-relax PNF techniques.

findings.claim: PNF typically produces greater flexibility gains than static stretching
findings.truth: Evidence does not support an unconditional superiority claim, and the lesson's single mechanism is not settled. One systematic review found comparisons with other stretches too low-certainty to determine whether PNF is more or less effective; proposed mechanisms are multiple. Option A: remove the comparison and causal account. Option B: recast both as tentative, technique-dependent possibilities.

summary: Six findings were recorded: four surgical fixes and two broader matters requiring curriculum or scientific judgement. All knowledge-check answer indices and match orders were checked.
